## What the evidence can and cannot support

Before forming any hypothesis I have to be explicit about the epistemic status of this input. I was given **only a magnitude ranking** (mean |IG| across all cells) from a nonlinear MLP. That means:

- **No direction.** I cannot tell whether a high-ranked gene is associated with *higher* or *lower* input resistance. Any sign I attach below comes from textbook biophysics, not from the data.
- **No decision rules, thresholds, or subgroup statistics** (no classifier was fit), so I cannot say "in subtype X, gene Y above level Z implies R_in < W".
- **No per-cell values**, so I cannot separate within-type variation from between-type variation.
- **Attribution ≠ causation**, and with correlated features (which scRNA-seq features always are) IG magnitude is smeared across co-expressed gene modules.

Most importantly: in Patch-seq data, input resistance differs *systematically* between transcriptomic GABAergic subtypes (Gouwens et al., 2020, *Nature*). Any gene that is a clean subtype marker will therefore receive high attribution **without being a regulator of R_in at all**. This confound is the single largest threat to interpretation here and I cannot resolve it from the ranking alone.

## Functional anatomy of the ranking

Reading the list as a whole, three groups stand out at the top:

1. **Subthreshold / resting K⁺ conductances.** Kcnq5 (#4, Kv7.5/M-current), Kcnmb4 (#7, BK β4 subunit), Kcna3 (#29, Kv1.3), Kcnd3 (#63, Kv4.3/A-type), Kcnh1 (#104), Kcnc1 (#126, Kv3.1), Kcnip4 (#132), Kcnn2 (#163, SK2), Kcnk3 (#281, TASK-1 leak), Kcnk2 (#346, TREK-1 leak), Kcnab3 (#329), Kcnip2 (#336). Two of the top ten features are K⁺ channel subunits — a clear over-representation relative to the ~2–3% base rate of K⁺ channel genes in the 1000-feature set.
2. **Tonic / resting ligand-gated and background conductances.** Gabrd (#61, δ-subunit → extrasynaptic tonic GABA conductance), Gabra5 (#166), Gabra4 (#98), Htr3a (#62), Asic2 (#135), Ano4 (#19), Grin2a (#143), Gria1 (#254), Adora1 (#289), Cnr1 (#38).
3. **Ion pumps / Ca²⁺ handling.** Fxyd6 (#1, FXYD-family Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase auxiliary subunit), Atp2b4 (#45, PMCA4), Cacna2d3 (#41) and Cacna2d1 (#50) (VGCC α2δ subunits), Cacng3 (#161), Orai2 (#164), Slc24a3 (#147).

Interleaved with these are canonical **subtype-identity** genes: Pvalb (#73), Lhx6 (#137), Dlx5/Dlx2/Dlx1 (#43/#157/#594), Tle4 (#10), Bcl11b (#55), Id2 (#83), Meis2 (#323), Adarb2 (#300), Cux2 (#145), Satb1/2, plus a large adhesion-molecule block (Pcdh8 #2, Cdh12 #35, Cdh9 #115, Kirrel3 #123, Igsf9b #67, Csmd3 #81, Cntnap5a/c, Dscaml1). Notably, the **top three features (Fxyd6, Pcdh8, Coro6) are not channels at all** — they are exactly the kind of low-expression, subtype-restricted genes the Allen taxonomy uses as marker genes. That is consistent with, though it does not prove, a substantial cell-type-identity component in the attribution.

## Best hypothesis

**Input resistance in mouse cortical GABAergic interneurons is set primarily by the summed resting and subthreshold K⁺ conductance of the cell — with Kcnq5 (M-current) and Kcnmb4-containing BK channels as the leading molecular candidates, supplemented by two-pore-domain leak channels (Kcnk2/Kcnk3), SK2 (Kcnn2) and A-type (Kcnd3) conductances — layered on a subtype-specific baseline that is itself encoded by transcription-factor and adhesion-molecule programs; Fxyd6-dependent modulation of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase is a plausible additional, non-channel contributor.**

In other words: the model's reliance on this gene set reflects the fact that GABAergic subtypes differ in their *complement of resting K⁺ conductances*, and that within-subtype variation in the same genes further tunes R_in. The non-channel top hits are most parsimoniously explained as identity markers that index which conductance regime a cell is in, rather than as independent regulators.

## Testable predictions

1. **Within-subtype correlation (the decisive test).** After regressing out transcriptomic subtype, per-cell expression of Kcnq5, Kcnmb4, Kcnk2/Kcnk3 and Kcnn2 should still correlate with measured R_in. If the correlation vanishes within subtype, the attribution is identity-driven, not regulatory. This requires the per-cell expression matrix and R_in values, which I was not given.
2. **Pharmacology.** In recorded interneurons, XE-991 (Kv7/M), paxilline or iberiotoxin (BK), and TREK/TASK blockers should each produce a measurable ΔR_in, and the size of ΔR_in should scale with that cell's expression of the corresponding gene.
3. **Fxyd6.** Knockdown of Fxyd6 should shift Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase activity and produce a small but detectable change in resting conductance/V_m — a non-channel route to R_in.
4. **Model-side control.** Retraining with subtype-mean expression subtracted should reveal which of the top-ranked features retain attribution; I predict the K⁺ channel block survives better than the adhesion/TF block.

## Relation to established literature

This is primarily **(a) a confirmation of established biophysics**, not a new mechanism. That resting input resistance is dominated by leak and subthreshold K⁺ conductances is textbook (Hille, *Ion Channels of Excitable Membranes*); KCNQ5 as a molecular correlate of M-current is established (Wang et al., 1998, *Science*; Schroeder et al., 2000, *JBC*); KCNMB4 is the predominant brain BK β-subunit (Brenner et al., 2000, *JBC*); KCNK-family two-pore channels underlie background/leak K⁺ currents (Lesage & Lazdunski, 2000; Talley et al., 2001); SK2 shapes subthreshold excitability (Stocker, 2004); δ-subunit-containing GABA_A receptors mediate tonic conductance that contributes to resting input resistance (Farrant & Nusser, 2005, *Nat Rev Neurosci*); FXYD proteins are established auxiliary regulators of the Na⁺/K⁺-ATPase (Sweadner & Rael, 2000; Geering, 2006), though FXYD6's specific neuronal function is comparatively poorly characterized.

The only genuinely **(b) new-testable** element is the *specific combination* proposed here — that Fxyd6 (pump modulation) and Kcnmb4/Kcnq5 (channel conductance) jointly index R_in within the same cells, and that the non-channel top hits are identity proxies rather than regulators. That is a falsifiable claim, but it is a hypothesis *generated* by the ranking, not one the ranking supports with evidence.

## Why confidence is limited

I could name a plausible gene set, but I cannot demonstrate from this input that (i) any of these genes changes R_in in the direction implied, (ii) the effect survives within-subtype control, or (iii) the ranking is not dominated by subtype identity. A magnitude-only, direction-free, classifier-free ranking is not sufficient to establish a specific regulatory mechanism. What would be needed: per-cell expression + R_in values, subtype labels, signed (not absolute) IG attributions, and within-subtype partial correlations.
